Name: Celtic Headhunting: Heads Hung from the Eaves and the Spiritual Belief in Valor
RagShortTexts: Gallic and Celtic berserkers saw the head as the seat of the human soul, spiritual power and the essence of life
They cut off the heads of enemy commanders, hung them from the horse's neck before the saddle, or preserved them for a long time by soaking them in cedar oil
After victory the enemy's skull was set in silver and used as a sacred cup for drinking mead, to awe foreign invaders
BaseText: The Cisalpine Boii and Insubrian Gallic warriors who fought alongside Hannibal on his campaigns in the Second Punic War kept the ancient and terrifying 'headhunting' custom (Headhunting). Celtic Druidic teaching firmly held that a person's soul, valor, wisdom and life force were all stored in the skull. After killing an enemy commander in front of the lines, a Gallic warrior would cut off the head and, shouting a victory cry, tie it beneath his horse's neck or on the point of his spear and ride about displaying it. Back in camp, they repeatedly rubbed and soaked the heads in precious cedar oil and pine resin to keep them from rotting, and displayed them on tent posts or the beams above their doors for guests to view for generations. In 216 BC, at the battle of the Litana forest, after the Boian Gauls ambushed and killed the Roman consul Postumius, they cleaned his skull, lined the inside of the cranium with pure gold, and made it the sacred golden cup in which the high Druid held the libation wine at holy rites.

Variants.Content: The head is a warrior's only true trophy! The golden skull of the Roman consul is filled with wine on our altar, and his strength already flows in the veins of the Boian warriors!

Utterly barbaric, man-eating demons! They dared to turn the skull of a noble Roman consul into a drinking cup; the sword of the Senate swears to tear out every oak grove of Cisalpine Gaul by the roots!

The Greeks seek perfect harmony in their statues, while the Celts nail the dried heads of their enemies to their doorposts to boast of their prowess. This is the wilderness we must hold back with the help of the great Roman shield.
